title: SoCal fishermen discover body floating in water yards from America's most haunted ship
excerpt: An investigation got underway after fishermen spotted the body and alerted Long Beach police.
content:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A man’s body was mysteriously found floating in the water near the Queen Mary in Long Beach on Monday night.

An investigation got underway after fishermen spotted the body and alerted Long Beach police.

Officers responded to reports of a body in the water in the 400 block of East Shoreline Village Drive at around 8:30 p.m. Monday, a police spokesperson told KTLA.

A witness identified as Ruben was at the scene with a friend when they saw the fishermen arrive.

“Two guys hopped out and the first thing they said was like, hey, there’s a dead body out there,’” Ruben told the TV station.

“We looked, and you see something floating for sure in the water.”

Emergency crews used a Long Beach Fire Department boat to recover the body.

Authorities have not yet released the identity of the deceased man.

The cause of his death has not been determined, and it remains unclear how he ended up in the water.

The California Post reached out to the Long Beach Police Department and the Port of Long Beach for additional information, but didn’t immediately hear back.

The Queen Mary is a retired British ocean liner that sailed the North Atlantic from 1936 to 1967. It remains a popular Southern California attraction, with an estimated 50 million people having visited.

The ship is now a hotel, venue for special events and museum. Measuring 1,019 feet long, it was built in Clydebank, Scotland, and became famous for its Art Deco design, transatlantic crossings and wartime troops.

In October, the Queen Mary was nominated by experts and voted on by readers as one of the spookiest places to stay.

Back in September, Long Beach took the first steps toward removing a Russian submarine, which has been moored alongside the Queen Mary since 1998, the Long Beach Post reported.

City officials sought information from contractors on how to haul away the deteriorating 299-foot vessel, including the logistics and eye-watering cost of sending it to a disposal site.
